title: A. v. B. AG — Competition Covenant and Contractual Penalty
lead: Business partners separating their interests restrict competitive use of shared brands while permitting indispensable notices. A later letter mixes transition information with promotion, prompting a penalty claim and opposing appeals over its reduction.

actors.name: A.
actors.role: Business owner and Arkadium chairman bound by the competition covenant.

actors.name: B. AG
actors.role: Personnel and management-services company claiming the contractual penalty.

actors.name: Arkadium AG
actors.role: New company taking over workers and placement processes.

actors.name: Sevenedge AG
actors.role: Company also named in the penalty clause.

proceedings: The Zug trial court dismissed the penalty claim.
The cantonal Obergericht found breach and awarded CHF 10,000 plus interest.
The Federal Supreme Court dismissed both civil appeals insofar as admissible and declined the subsidiary constitutional appeal.
limits: This transforms the canonical September 2024 brief without a fresh audit or subsequent Swiss-law certification. Party names remain anonymized as in the source. Pinpoints follow its facts, reasoning sections, and dispositive orders. The assigned translation’s June 1988 header is erroneous; the decision is from 2024. Contractual fidelity is distinct from the translation’s broader good-faith wording.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: A business separation preserves names while allowing necessary notices
sections.cue: What did the covenant forbid and except?
paragraphs: B. AG supplied personnel, strategy, management, and planning services under Construction21, Care21, and PrimeSelect. On December 11, 2020, its directors and A., chairman of newly formed Arkadium AG, jointly notified construction customers that Arkadium would take over employees, ongoing candidate-placement processes, and customer management retroactively from October 1.

A week later, A., B. AG, its directors, and others arranged share purchases to separate related interests. A. sold his B. AG shares to that company and a director-controlled company; B. AG sold him its holdings in a company he led.

Clauses 5.1–5.2 barred A. and connected businesses from competitively using Prime, GetTemp, Construction, Care, and 21, presenting themselves under B. AG’s brands, or suggesting the former association. Exceptions allowed past employment in résumés and social media and information indispensable to legal or contractual obligations to outsiders, including data-protection explanations and necessary implementation changes. Clause 5.3 imposed CHF 100,000 per individual violation, payable by A. and/or Sevenedge AG without releasing compliance or further-damage liability.

sections.title: The expert letter combines transition information with advertising
sections.cue: What presentation triggered the penalty demand?
paragraphs: On January 11, 2021, A. wrote to Construction21’s experts, workers placed with construction businesses. The letter announced Arkadium’s takeover of Construction21’s operational business and existing employment contracts. Its heading placed CONSTRUCTION21 beside Arkadium, and A. signed with Arkadium AG/B. AG and his chairman’s title.

It also described Arkadium as a leading Construction & Property headhunter and advertised specialties. B. AG claimed unauthorized competitive use and sought CHF 100,000 plus five-percent interest, initially from January 12, 2021.

sections.title: The cantonal courts disagree, and both parties seek federal review
sections.cue: Which award and appeal routes were at stake?
paragraphs: The Zug trial court dismissed on September 20, 2023. On February 23, 2024, the Obergericht partly allowed B. AG’s appeal, found violations, and awarded CHF 10,000 plus five-percent interest from November 19, 2021, rejecting the balance.

A.’s civil appeal sought dismissal, alternatively CHF 500 or CHF 1,000, or remand. B. AG’s civil appeal sought CHF 100,000 with the later interest date or remand; it also filed a subsidiary constitutional appeal. Each opposed the other.

The Federal Supreme Court consolidated the cases. Timely civil review of the final cantonal judgment was available and met the CHF 30,000 threshold, so subsidiary constitutional review was unavailable. Factual review generally accepted cantonal findings unless a substantiated, outcome-relevant claim showed arbitrariness or another qualifying error. Additional facts required identification of their proper introduction below, not a fresh factual narrative.

sections.title: Truthful transition information can still exceed the agreed exception
sections.cue: Why did necessity decide the breach question?
paragraphs: Contract interpretation first sought actual shared intent; absent proved agreement, the principle of trust supplied objective contextual meaning. Here the parties’ shared understanding permitted an expert notice only to the extent indispensable to informing outsiders.

The lower court accepted the takeover description as not incorrect: B. AG identified no Construction21 operations it conducted or intended at the letter date, and transferred processes and infrastructure substantially matched that description. Later renewed activity did not change it. The December joint letter also supported neutral notice.

But announcing operational takeover twice went beyond necessity. A. could explain organizational changes and direct candidates in ongoing placements to Arkadium from October 1. He justified neither broader wording nor departure from the earlier limited title. In that setting, CONSTRUCTION21 in the letterhead and B. AG in the signature were unauthorized.

The leading-headhunter claim and specialty list promoted Arkadium beyond neutral process and management information, suggesting candidates now belonged with it. Even one promotional use could exceed the exception. Truth and an interest in retaining an expensive database’s experts supplied no contractual permission. An additional unasserted violation identified below was disregarded rather than added on appeal.

A. did not establish absence of fault. Business experience and deliberate revision of the earlier letter supported at least conditional intent. Repeating that transfer was real and database notices were permissible did not rebut the narrower unnecessary-promotion finding.

sections.title: The penalty matures without damage but can be reduced for excessiveness
sections.cue: Why was neither full enforcement nor a token award warranted?
paragraphs: Swiss Code of Obligations article 163 allowed freely set penalties but required discretionary reduction of excessive amounts. Respect for contractual fidelity required restraint, particularly assessment of gross disproportion to the creditor’s enforcement interest at breach. Relevant factors included duration and nature, fault, severity, protected interest, economic circumstances, dependence, and business experience. Article 161(1) allowed a penalty without actual damage, but no damage or demonstrated risk still mattered to reduction.

The cantonal findings characterized a very minor, one-time breach with recurrence practically excluded. B. AG had shown neither harm nor risk. A single candidate email was not causally explained; advertising effects, database or placement numbers, and lost experts were unsubstantiated. Precise numerical damages were unnecessary, but some substantive answer to A.’s no-consequences position was required.

B. AG’s own reading of that email did not prove arbitrariness or multiple confused candidates. Registered marks, reciprocity, sophisticated parties, and transaction size did not show why CHF 50,000 or CHF 100,000 matched this breach. Harmful intent was asserted late without support, other confusion claims departed from the record, and profit to A. was not shown. Reduction did not reverse proof burdens or exceed requested relief because A. expressly sought it.

Conversely, A.’s no-operations and no-effects points had already been weighed. They did not remove the penalty’s punitive function in a financially substantial transaction. CHF 10,000 remained meaningful and appropriate; his proposed CHF 500 per violation totaling CHF 1,000 was rejected, not adopted as a rate.

sections.title: Both civil appeals fail and separate appellate costs are allocated
paragraphs: On September 24, 2024, the First Civil Law Division dismissed both civil appeals insofar as admissible and declined the subsidiary constitutional appeal. The CHF 10,000 penalty with five-percent interest from November 19, 2021 remained. President Jametti and Judges Kiss and Rüedi sat, with Matt as clerk; no separate opinions or numerical vote were reported.

A. bore CHF 2,000 federal costs and B. AG CHF 5,000. Party compensation was CHF 2,500 owed by A. to B. AG and CHF 6,000 owed by B. AG to A.; offset left B. AG owing CHF 3,500. Those appellate sums were distinct from the contractual penalty.
